summary: Defines a new DNS OPCODE for DNS Stateful Operations, which use TLV messages in persistent stateful sessions. Three TLVs handle session timeouts, termination and encryption padding, and a framework allows more to be added.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS normally answers one question at a time over a short connection. But a client that keeps a connection open can save the cost of setting it up each time, and can receive messages the server sends on its own. This RFC defines the extra messages that make that possible: the client asks for the settings it wants, the server says what settings the client must use, and both ends can keep the connection alive.

questions: what is the dso retry delay tlv
subtitle: A DNS operation for managing the settings of a long-lived DNS connection.

tldr.problem: DNS over TCP and DNS over TLS can hold a connection open, but the existing extension mechanism, EDNS(0), has strictly per-message semantics. A server therefore cannot tell a client how long to keep an idle connection open, and cannot send the client a message of its own unless the client happens to be waiting for a reply.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new DNS opcode, DSO with value 6, whose messages carry type-length-value records. The first record in a message is the primary one and says what the message does; the other records carry extra information. Three records are defined: Keepalive, which negotiates the session timeouts, Retry Delay, which tells a client not to come back for a while, and Encryption Padding, which adds filler bytes.
tldr.outcome: A client and a server can now agree, out of band, how long a connection should stay open, keep it alive through NAT gateways and firewalls, and let the server initiate messages. The document also updates the DNS-over-TCP specification, which defined a session only as a connection with an idle timeout.

today: RFC 8490 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It adds a new DNS opcode to RFC 1035 and updates the session handling in RFC 7766. The older keepalive option it replaces is RFC 7828.

sections.title: Why DNS Needed a New Operation
sections.content:
DNS most commonly operates over UDP, but it can also operate over streaming transports: the original DNS specification defines DNS-over-TCP, and a profile for DNS-over-TLS has been specified. These transports can offer persistent long-lived sessions, so when they are used for transporting DNS messages it is of benefit to have a mechanism that can establish parameters associated with those sessions, such as timeouts. In such situations it is also advantageous to support server-initiated messages, such as DNS Push Notifications.

The existing Extension Mechanism for DNS is explicitly defined to have only per-message semantics. Although EDNS(0) has been used to signal at least one session-related parameter, the edns-tcp-keepalive option, the result is less than optimal because of the restrictions imposed by the EDNS(0) semantics and the lack of server-initiated signalling. For example, a server cannot arbitrarily instruct a client to close a connection, because the server can only send EDNS(0) options in responses to queries that contained EDNS(0) options.

This document defines a new DNS OPCODE for DNS Stateful Operations, with a value of 6. DSO messages communicate operations within persistent stateful sessions using Type Length Value syntax, and the document defines an initial set of three TLVs used to manage session timeouts, termination and encryption padding. All three TLVs defined here are mandatory for all implementations of DSO, and further TLVs may be defined in additional specifications.

The format of a DSO message differs from the traditional DNS message format used for standard queries and responses. The standard twelve-byte header is used, but the four count fields are set to zero and their corresponding sections are not present; the DSO data is appended to the end of the header. The new format has distinct advantages over an RR-based format because it is more explicit and more compact, each TLV definition is specific to its use case and contains no redundant or overloaded fields, and it completely avoids conflating DNS Stateful Operations with normal DNS operations or with existing EDNS(0)-based functionality. A goal of this approach is to avoid the operational issues that have befallen EDNS(0), particularly those relating to middlebox behaviour.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing way to add options to a DNS message only works one message at a time, so the server can only speak when the client asks something. DSO gives the two ends a channel of their own for talking about the connection, including the server starting a conversation.

sections.title: Which Transports Can Carry It
sections.content:
DNS Stateful Operations apply where it is useful to maintain an open session between a DNS client and server, where the transport allows such a session to be maintained, and where the transport guarantees in-order delivery of messages on which DSO depends. Two specific transports meet those requirements: DNS-over-TCP and DNS-over-TLS. In the case of DNS-over-TLS there is no mechanism for upgrading from DNS-over-TCP to DNS-over-TLS mid-connection, so a connection is either DNS-over-TCP from the start or DNS-over-TLS from the start.

DSO is not applicable to transports that cannot support clean session semantics or that do not guarantee in-order delivery. While in principle such a transport could be constructed over UDP, the current specification of DNS-over-UDP does not provide in-order delivery or session semantics and hence cannot be used. Similarly DNS-over-HTTP cannot be used, because HTTP has its own mechanism for managing sessions, which is incompatible with the mechanism specified here. Only DNS-over-TCP and DNS-over-TLS are currently defined for use with DNS Stateful Operations, and other transports may be added in the future if they meet the requirements.

The use cases are session management and long-lived subscriptions. For session management, using DSO Sessions for stub-to-recursive DNS-over-TLS is more flexible for both the client and the server than attempting to manage sessions using just the edns-tcp-keepalive option. For long-lived subscriptions, DNS-based Service Discovery has evolved into a naturally session-based mechanism where long-lived subscriptions lend themselves to push mechanisms as opposed to polling. A general use case is that DNS traffic is often bursty but session establishment can be expensive, and one challenge with long-lived connections is sustaining sufficient traffic to maintain NAT and firewall state. To mitigate this, the document introduces the concept of DSO keepalive traffic, which carries no DNS data and is not considered activity in the classic DNS sense, but serves to maintain state in middleboxes and to assure the client and server that they still have connectivity to each other.
sections.plainLanguage: DSO needs a transport that delivers messages in order and can stay open, so it works over TCP and over TLS, and not over plain UDP or over HTTP. Its purpose is to let a client and a server agree on how long to keep a connection open and to keep that connection alive through the firewalls that sit between them.

sections.title: Establishing a Session
sections.content:
A DSO Session is established over a connection by the client sending a DSO request message and receiving a response with a matching MESSAGE ID and RCODE set to NOERROR, indicating that the request was successful. In some environments it may be known in advance by external means that both client and server support DSO, and in those cases either client or server may initiate DSO messages at any time, which is referred to as implicit session establishment. In the typical case a server will not know in advance whether a client supports DSO, so a server MUST NOT initiate DSO request messages or DSO unidirectional messages until a session has been mutually established by at least one successful request and response exchange initiated by the client, which is referred to as explicit establishment.

Once a session has been established, either end may unilaterally send appropriate DSO messages at any time, so either the client or the server may be the initiator of a message. Because a server that supports DSO must return NOERROR for a Keepalive TLV request, the Keepalive TLV is an ideal candidate for use in establishing a session. For clients that implement only the DSO types defined in this base specification, sending a Keepalive TLV is the only request message available to initiate a session.

Failure is handled in a defined way. If the response RCODE is NOTIMP, or in practice any value other than NOERROR or DSOTYPENI, the client must assume the server does not implement DSO at all, and may continue sending DNS messages but must not issue further DSO messages on that connection. If the RCODE is DSOTYPENI, meaning the server supports DSO but does not implement the type of the primary TLV, then a session is not considered established, but the client may try other DSO messages such as the Keepalive.

When a DSO message reaches a server that does not recognize the DSO opcode, the server might send no response or might drop the connection. If no response arrives within 30 seconds the client must forcibly abort the connection, because there is no specification covering the server's state in that case; by disconnecting and reconnecting the client ensures the server is in a known state before sending subsequent requests. If the server drops the connection, the client should mark that service instance as not supporting DSO and not attempt a DSO connection for some period of time, at least an hour, after the failed attempt.
sections.plainLanguage: The client starts by sending a keepalive request and waits for the server's answer. If the answer says the server does not do DSO at all, the client stops trying and carries on with plain DNS. If the server simply never answers, the client hangs up after thirty seconds and reconnects, because it cannot know what state the server is in.

sections.title: The Message Format
sections.content:
A DSO message begins with the standard twelve-byte DNS message header with the OPCODE field set to 6. Unlike standard DNS messages, the question, answer, authority records and additional records sections are not present, and the corresponding count fields MUST be set to zero on transmission. If a DSO message is received where any of the count fields are not zero, then a FORMERR MUST be returned.

The MESSAGE ID field MUST be zero in a DSO unidirectional message, and in a DSO request message it MUST be a unique nonzero value that the initiator is not currently using for any other active operation on the connection. Whether a message is a request or a unidirectional message is determined only by the specification for the primary TLV: an acknowledgement cannot be requested by including a nonzero MESSAGE ID in a message required to be unidirectional, nor prevented by sending a MESSAGE ID of zero in a message required to be a request, and a responder that receives either such malformed message MUST treat it as a fatal error and forcibly abort the connection immediately. In a DSO response message the QR bit MUST be one and the MESSAGE ID MUST NOT be zero, and MUST contain a copy of the value in the request being answered; a response with a zero MESSAGE ID is a fatal error. The Z bits are currently unused in DSO messages and MUST be set to zero on transmission and ignored on reception.

The RCODE of a response may be NOERROR, meaning the operation was processed successfully, FORMERR for a format error, SERVFAIL when the server failed to process the request because of a problem with the server, NOTIMP meaning DSO is not supported, REFUSED meaning the operation was declined for policy reasons, or DSOTYPENI meaning the primary TLV's type is not implemented.

The DSO data follows the header and is expressed using TLV syntax. Every TLV has a 16-bit DSO-TYPE giving its type, a 16-bit DSO-LENGTH giving the size of the data in bytes, and the data itself, which the generic DSO machinery treats as an opaque blob. The first TLV in a request or unidirectional message is the primary TLV and determines the nature of the operation being performed, including whether the message is a request or a unidirectional operation; other TLVs follow it and are additional TLVs. An unrecognized primary TLV results in a DSOTYPENI error response, while unrecognized additional TLVs are silently ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A DSO message is an ordinary DNS header with the query and answer sections left out, followed by a list of records. Each record starts with a number saying what it is and a number saying how long it is. The first record decides what the message is asking for; the rest add detail.

sections.title: The Inactivity Timeout and the Keepalive Interval
sections.content:
The inactivity timeout exists so that the server can balance the cost of setting up new sessions against the cost of maintaining inactive ones. A server with abundant capacity can offer a high inactivity timeout, so clients can keep a speculative session open for a long time and save the cost of establishing a new one. A server with scarce memory can offer a low timeout, so clients promptly close sessions when they have no outstanding operations and create a new one later.

When the inactivity timeout is reached the client MUST begin closing the idle connection, though it may close a session at any time. If the inactivity timeout elapses without any operation active on the session, the client MUST close the connection gracefully. If too much time elapses without any operation active, the server MUST consider the client delinquent and forcibly abort the session; what counts as too much is five seconds or twice the current inactivity timeout value, whichever is greater. With the default value of 15 seconds, a client that has not closed its connection after 30 seconds of inactivity is disconnected.

An operation being active includes a query waiting for a response, an update waiting for a response, or an active long-lived operation, but not a Keepalive message exchange itself. A Keepalive message exchange resets only the keepalive timer, not the inactivity timer, so that a client cannot keep a session alive with keepalives alone.

The keepalive interval exists to generate enough messages to maintain state in middleboxes such as NAT gateways and firewalls, and to let the client and server check that they still have connectivity. If the keepalive interval elapses without any DNS message being sent or received, the client MUST send a DSO Keepalive message. If twice the keepalive interval elapses without any DNS message, the server SHOULD consider the client delinquent and forcibly abort the session. A server MUST NOT send a Keepalive message with a keepalive interval value less than ten seconds, because a single lost packet could then make the server abort the connection. By default it is RECOMMENDED that clients request and servers grant a keepalive interval of 60 minutes, which gives reasonably timely detection of an abrupt disconnect and is enough to keep state in firewalls and NAT gateways that follow the recommended idle timeout of at least 2 hours and 4 minutes. An inactivity timeout or keepalive interval of 0xFFFFFFFF means infinity, and the largest finite value the current Keepalive TLV supports is 0xFFFFFFFE, about 49.7 days.
sections.plainLanguage: Two timers run. The inactivity timer says how long the session may sit doing nothing useful, after which the client closes it. The keepalive timer says how long the session may sit silent in any way, after which the client must send something to show it is still there. A keepalive does not count as useful activity, so the two cannot keep each other going forever.

sections.title: The Three Base TLVs
sections.content:
The Keepalive TLV, with DSO-TYPE 1, performs two functions. Primarily it establishes the values for the session timeouts, and incidentally it resets the keepalive timer, so it can be used as a kind of no-op message for the purpose of keeping a session alive. The client requests the session timeout values it wants and the server acknowledges with the values it requires the client to use. Its data is two 32-bit values in milliseconds, the inactivity timeout and the keepalive interval. The server's values are the ones that count, which is modelled after the DHCP protocol, where the client requests a lease lifetime but the server decides the lifetime actually granted. A Keepalive message sent by a client must be a request with a nonzero MESSAGE ID; a Keepalive message sent by a server must be unidirectional with a MESSAGE ID of zero, and no client response to it is required or allowed.

The Retry Delay TLV, with DSO-TYPE 2, carries a 32-bit value in milliseconds within which the initiator MUST NOT retry the operation or reconnect to the server. Used as the primary TLV in a unidirectional server-to-client message, it instructs the client to close the session and not to reconnect for that interval, and the RCODE in the header indicates the reason: NOERROR for a routine shutdown or restart, FORMERR for a client request too badly malformed for the session to continue, SERVFAIL for a server overloaded and shedding load, REFUSED for a server that has been reconfigured and can no longer perform one or more of the long-lived operations, and NOTAUTH for a server that has lost authority over the names in question. Used as a response additional TLV, it tells the initiator not to retry just that failed operation. A client MUST NOT send a Retry Delay message to a server.

The Encryption Padding TLV, with DSO-TYPE 3, can only be used as an additional or response additional TLV, and is only applicable when the DSO transport layer uses encryption such as TLS. Its data is an optional variable-length field of unspecified values, and a length of zero provides for four bytes of padding. The padding bytes should be set to zero, though other values may be used where there is a concern that the padded message could be subject to compression before encryption, and padding bytes of any value must be accepted on receipt. If a request is received with an Encryption Padding TLV then the response must also include one.
sections.plainLanguage: Three operations are defined. Keepalive carries the two timers and doubles as a way of saying nothing. Retry Delay says do not come back for a while, and the reason is in the message's result code. Encryption Padding adds filler bytes so that the length of the message gives nothing away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If this mechanism is to be used with DNS-over-TLS, then these messages are subject to the same constraints as any other DNS-over-TLS messages and MUST NOT be sent in the clear before the TLS session is established.

The RFC also notes that a DSO message cannot contain a valid EDNS(0) option, because the ARCOUNT field must be zero, and cannot contain a TSIG record for the same reason. If functionality provided by EDNS(0) options is desired for DSO messages, one or more new DSO TLVs need to be defined to carry the necessary information. The edns-tcp-keepalive option is explicitly prohibited in any messages sent on a DSO session, because it is obsoleted by the functionality provided by the DSO Keepalive operation; a message that contains it is a fatal error.
sections.plainLanguage: Over TLS the DSO messages are protected like any other DNS message. Because the DSO header leaves no room for the usual DNS extensions, DSO defines its own padding record instead of using the standard one, and it forbids the older keepalive option because the DSO keepalive replaces it.

messages.label: KEEPALIVE REQUEST
messages.note: A DSO request with a nonzero MESSAGE ID, asking for the session timeouts the client wants.

messages.label: KEEPALIVE RESPONSE
messages.note: The server's own values for the inactivity timeout and the keepalive interval.

messages.label: DNS QUERY
messages.note: Ordinary DNS messages continue over the same connection.

messages.label: PUSH NOTIFICATION
messages.note: Now that the session is established, the server can send a message of its own.

viz.caption: THE DNS HEADER AS USED BY DSO

fields.name: MESSAGE ID
fields.desc: Zero for a unidirectional message, nonzero for a request and its response.

fields.name: QR
fields.desc: Zero in a request or unidirectional message, one in a response.

fields.name: Z
fields.desc: Unused in DSO messages. Must be zero on transmission and ignored on reception.

fields.name: RCODE
fields.desc: The result of the operation in a response.

fields.name: QDCOUNT, ANCOUNT, NSCOUNT, ARCOUNT
fields.desc: All four count fields must be zero, so none of the usual DNS sections are present.

data.title: DSO TLV
data.code:
DSO-TYPE   : 16 bits, the type of this TLV
DSO-LENGTH : 16 bits, the size of DSO-DATA in bytes
DSO-DATA   : type-specific; the DSO machinery treats it as
              an opaque blob and does not interpret it

items.title: Inactivity timeout
items.text: How long the session may sit with no useful activity. The client closes it when the time is up, and the server aborts it if the client has not.

items.title: Keepalive interval
items.text: How long the session may sit with no DNS message at all. The client must send a keepalive by then, and it must be at least ten seconds.

items.title: Two different defaults
items.text: Both default to 15 seconds, but the recommended keepalive interval is 60 minutes.

items.title: A keepalive is not activity
items.text: A keepalive resets only the keepalive timer, not the inactivity timer, so the two cannot lock each other in a loop.

cells: Sets the session timeout values and resets the keepalive timer. May appear in early data.
Tells the client not to retry for a while. Not permitted in early data.
Adds filler bytes. Only usable as an additional TLV.
